blocks.text: The five d orbitals are dxy, dxz, dyz, dx2-y2 and dz2. Four have a cloverleaf shape (four lobes in a plane) and dz2 has two lobes and a ring. In an isolated atom all five have the same energy: they are degenerate. Their shapes and directions decide the bonding, colour and magnetic properties of transition metals.

blocks.alt: Three panels with dashed axes. d_xy: four lobes between the x and y axes. d_x2-y2: four lobes along the x and y axes. d_z2: two lobes along the z axis with a ring round the middle in the xy plane. Two shades mark the opposite phases.
blocks.caption: Shapes of three 3d orbitals (original sketch for the learning outcome on the 3dxy and 3dz2 orbitals).
blocks.long_description: There are five 3d orbitals. Four of them (dxy, dxz, dyz and dx2-y2) have four lobes in a plane, a cloverleaf shape: dxy, dxz and dyz point between the axes, while dx2-y2 points along the x and y axes. The fifth, dz2, has two lobes along the z axis and a ring (doughnut) of electron density round the middle. Because the orbitals point in different directions, ligands approaching along the axes affect them differently.

blocks.title: Degenerate and non-degenerate orbitals
blocks.text: Degenerate orbitals have the same energy. When ligands approach a metal ion to form a complex, their electric field splits the five d orbitals into two sets of different energy (non-degenerate). The energy gap between the sets is written delta E.
In an octahedral complex (six ligands), such as [Ti(H2O)6]3+, the d orbitals split into three lower-energy orbitals (dxy, dxz, dyz) and two higher-energy orbitals (dx2-y2, dz2).

blocks.alt: Energy diagram. Left: five equal (degenerate) d boxes of the free ion, one holding an electron. Middle: in the complex the boxes split into three lower (dxy, dxz, dyz) and two higher (dx2-y2, dz2), separated by delta E; the electron is in a lower box. Light of energy delta E = h nu moves it to an upper box (right).
blocks.caption: Splitting of the d orbitals in an octahedral field (original diagram after Figure 18.4).
blocks.long_description: In an octahedral complex such as [Ti(H2O)6]3+ the six ligands approach along the x, y and z axes. The dx2-y2 and dz2 orbitals point straight at them and rise in energy; the dxy, dxz and dyz orbitals point between them and fall. The gap between the two sets is delta E. Ti3+ has one 3d electron; when it absorbs light of energy delta E it is promoted from a lower to an upper orbital.

blocks.text: In a tetrahedral complex (four ligands), such as [CuCl4]2-, the splitting is inverted: three higher-energy orbitals (dxy, dxz, dyz) and two lower-energy orbitals (dx2-y2, dz2). The splitting is smaller than in octahedral complexes.

blocks.alt: Energy diagram for [CuCl4]2- (d9). Five degenerate boxes with nine electrons split into two lower boxes (dx2-y2, dz2), both full, and three higher boxes (dxy, dxz, dyz) holding five electrons, with a smaller gap delta E. Absorbing light moves one electron from a lower to an upper box.
blocks.caption: Splitting of the d orbitals in a tetrahedral field (original diagram after Figure 18.5).
blocks.long_description: In a tetrahedral complex the four ligands do not lie on the axes, so the splitting is inverted: dxy, dxz and dyz rise and dx2-y2 and dz2 fall. With only four ligands, none pointing straight at an orbital, the splitting is smaller than in an octahedral complex.

blocks.prompt: Which d orbitals are higher in energy in an octahedral complex, and why?
blocks.explanation: dx2-y2 and dz2, because their lobes point straight at the ligands on the axes and are repelled most.

items: Five d orbitals are degenerate in a free ion; ligands split them by delta E.
Octahedral: 3 lower, 2 higher. Tetrahedral: 2 lower, 3 higher, smaller gap.
